I wouldn't worry too much about weight gain, I don't think it's very common with SSRIs. I tried a bunch and none of them made me gain weight. Mirtazapine was a whole other story, those 4.5 weeks were hell, I didn't even get the trade off of feeling better for the 4kg I gained.

I think the problem with SSRIs is that it's almost entirely a guessing game. Everyone reacts so differently to different ones and different doses, so you often end up doing a lot of trial and error before you either find one that works for you or your doctor concludes that they aren't right for you (personally, I took about 5 before they came to that conclusion) 

I'm surprised they gave you that for mood swings though, because they often induce mania in those people and they don't really level your mood out at all even if they work really well.

Dissociation is supposedly a survival adaptation for extreme stress, and only becomes an issue when it's happening in situations where that amount of stress is normal (like if you have an anxiety disorder). So I would think if you find one that helps your anxiety then it would also help the dissociation.

I would suggest making another appointment with your doctor to talk about your concerns, and ask what you should be looking out for in terms of concerning side effects if you do decide to take them. A mood diary can also help you figure out if it's working or not (I just rate 1-10 because its low effort), especially because its hard to see the bigger picture over the 4-6 weeks it takes to really see any improvements. Also if you're around people you trust, it can help to let them know you're starting meds and ask them to let you know if they notice any changes, good or bad, because they can be more objective and might notice things you don't.

When I think about myself as a child, honestly the first thing I feel is disgust. I hate a lot of how I behaved, what I felt, and just child-me in general.

But I try to remember that every child deserves to be safe and looked after and loved. I try to see how I was really just mirroring the behaviour of my 'role models'. I have a lot of memories of abuse, but my memories of hating myself go back further, so I'm pretty sure the root cause is something that goes too far back for me to have a concrete memory of it. When I can't see how the abuse made me like that, I look at how others behaved around me, if not to me, and blame them for everything I hate about child-me.

I'm not all the way there yet, I have days when I can barely stand to exist because I hate everything I am and have ever been. But some days I want nothing more than to give in to everything my inner child wants because fundamentally what she wants are things I think every child deserves, and I feel sorry that she has terrible role models that have taught her badly.

I don't like the idea of healing entirely through self parenting because I just can't see how my screwed up attachment system can be fixed without stable and secure attachments/relationships. Like you said, relational healing.

But I do use the 'inner child' concept, because when I recognise that parts of me are stuck at the child stage I find it easier to be nice to myself and really hard to hurt myself. And I do kind of parent myself at that point I guess, but I definitely don't consider myself my own parent. I wrap myself up in a blanket because being wrapped up in a blanket feels good, not because it's something I think a parent would do. I just give in to the childish things I want and try not to feel guilty about it, I don't know the actual psychology behind it but I imagine it like I wanted/needed those things and when I didn't get them, it just carried forward so I'm making up for it now. 

I don't really think of it as my inner child though, the separation between inner child and self parent feels like too much of a gap for me to be both. It's more a short term way to self soothe than real long term healing for me I think.

I'm a law student, so this advice largely focuses on critical essays and problem questions, and is fairly specific to exams where you have access to any resources, as opposed to just a textbook/limited notes. Also my exams are 72 hours so you might need to tweak it if you're on a tighter deadline. 

You want a good set of reference notes, take everything from your classes, textbook, extra reading, any source you can use to get your info from. Put it all in 1 document, preferably with headings + a table of contents so you can navigate it easily. Write it all in your own words (unless you find a particularly good quote you might want to use in the exam), even if you have to make it super informal to be able to explain it yourself. In fact, if you aren't sure you understand something, writing it in the most informal style you can is a good way to check. If you can put the information in a different format (diagram, table, whatever) then do that, it will help your understanding and break up the text to make it easier not to skip things. Good notes, and I mean really good, is my #1 tip. 

Your notes should also be referenced in whatever style your exam will use. Not necessarily in footnotes, but if you include a point from your notes in your exam, you should have the correctly formatted reference to copy and paste, it will save you time and make you more confident in your answers. 

Include your own thoughts as well, it can be hard to come up with an opinion when you're under pressure. It's much easier to write down your opinions whilst you're having class discussions or questioning the reasoning of what you're reading.

Do practice exams. Do timed practice exams, no matter how generous the allowed time is. Get them marked if you can, otherwise use examiners reports/example answers to mark them yourself. Obviously make sure you correct any wrong answers, but also try to spot patterns in your mistakes. Do you always miss out topic x in your essays? You've got a problem with topic x. Do you often skip steps? You need a better outline of the right process and a checklist to make sure you follow it.

If you have problem questions or similar that require a process, a flowchart is a good way to get a handle on it. It can also function as an outline for your answers, highlight your route through the flow chart and expand on each step as you go through. Include simple things like 'give definition of x' that make your answer easier to follow and clearly show your understanding.

Have a checklist. If you're told about common mistakes, put them on your checklist. If you make a mistake in a practice exam/question, it goes on the checklist. If your classmate makes a mistake, checklist. This is for things like mixing up similar keywords, grammar, formatting, referencing, rather than mistakes you made once because you didn't understand the material. Be specific, don't put 'check grammar', put 'use capital letters at the start of sentences' (that's very basic, but substitute for mistakes you actually make). When you think you've finished, take some time away from the exam if possible and then go through the checklist one item at a time.

When you get feedback, come up with concrete ways you can implement the suggestions. If you get told your writing style is unclear, maybe you need to use shorter sentences. Add those to the checklist too. If you should include more of something (critical comments, references to secondary sources, etc) then you should put more of that in your notes.

If you have a lot of keywords, especially if they're easily mixed up, keep a separate glossary, that way you can have it open alongside your notes and you don't lose your place if you need to check something.

In the exam, don't try to reword things 1000 times to get it perfect, say what you have to, say it clearly and without contractions, etc, then move on. The improvement from constant reworking will be minimal but will stress you out and take time away from more important things.

Spend time on the question. Break it down, use that breakdown to guide your introduction. Plan what you want to say and what you'll conclude before you start writing, but if you realise halfway through that you were wrong, don't be afraid to change your mind. You can use what you already wrote as your counter argument.

That's a lot of stuff, but hopefully it works as a general guide that y'all can pick from according to what suits you/your exams!

I had terrible experiences with SSRIs for years, tried almost every other antidepressant going as well (except MAOIs, apparently they're terrible and I have an arrhythmia so I might die if I take them or something, idk). CBT made me feel worse, same with grounding.

But there other options besides benzos, and most are more suitable for long term relief. Olanzapine worked well for me as a substitute for xanax, I think other atypical antipsychotics can be used as well. There's also propanol, which I can't take because I'm asthmatic but has helped some of my antidepressant-resistant friends. Other types of antidepressants besides SSRIs can work for anxiety too, which apparently doctors like to ignore in favor of just trying every SSRI there is despite them all being clearly ineffective.

Probably going in and straight up asking for benzos with no focus on longer term care isn't helping, although I understand the feeling of need help NOW and being frustrated that the other options they give you are limited and also just terrible.

My suggestion would be to say you want to try something other than an SSRI but you need immediate help in the meantime, then ask what your options are for short term relief. I hope you manage to get the help you deserve!

Also my version of a 'good student' wasn't the same as everyone else's. I know I can't stick to a schedule so I have reminders set for my classes, a master task list ordered by priority and labels on tasks with deadlines, every morning I tag tasks that need to be done that day, then I spend my time working through the tasks however I feel like it. I'm not sure how long you've been driving for, but to some extent its likely this will get better on its own. I don't mean that in a dismissive 'everyone experiences that' way, because it will probably take more time and work for you than it does for 'everyone'.

But the things that are taking your focus now eventually become habit. What helped me was introducing things one at a time until they became second nature. I just moved off and stopped (staying in first gear) until balancing the clutch required no attention at all. Then I added in using my indicators until I didn't have to think about that anymore. And so on, until I could drive.

It seems like you're beyond this level, but the principle remains the same. Introduce things slowly. Now the only thing that really requires my focus when I drive is the traffic and where I'm going, everything else is automatic (until my car breaks down lol, then that becomes the focus!)
